ASRSN:2097977.n: During ILS RWY 10 approach aircraft flew over drone at 2000 ft and 7nm from the runway threshold. Drone was grey and with 4 rotors.
ASRSN:2097977.s: During an ILS approach to Runway 10, the aircraft flew over a grey, four-rotor drone at 2,000 feet and 7 nautical miles from the runway threshold. The pilot reported the encounter but provided no further details on the cause or outcome.

ASRSN:2097995.n: ZZZ takeoff XXR. Wind was 320/21/G39. The Captain was flying. He stabilized thrust at 40%, applied takeoff thrust 82.7. Prior to 80 kts. around 40-50 kts., aircraft pulled hard to the left of centerline roughly 20-25 ft. He rejected takeoff and exited runway at Taxiway 1. It appeared that we had a wind gust hit the tail causing the aircraft to weathervane to the left. He applied full right rudder and had little authority due to low airspeed. He closed thrust levers and regained centerline. Exited the runway and contacted Dispatch.
ASRSN:2097995.s: The Captain rejected a takeoff on ZZZ at XXR due to a wind gust causing the aircraft to weathervane left at 40–50 kts. Low airspeed limited rudder authority, forcing an exit at Taxiway 1 after thrust was closed.

ASRSN:2098016.n: During cruise we had the Generator One Drive light illuminated. We followed the QRH procedure but, the APU would not start and illuminated the APU Fault light. We diverted to ZZZ, our nearest suitable airport and landed with no other issues. ATC [requested priority handling] for us on the arrival into ZZZ.Suggestions: Occasionally start the APU at altitude to ensure that they will start inflight. Drive light illuminated in flight. The FO and I followed the QRH guidance and attempted to start the APU. We received an APU Fault light. This requires landing at the nearest suitable airport. We diverted to ZZZ. ATC [requested priority handling] on our behalf while we were on approach. I contacted Dispatch in flight via ACARS with the Maintenance and divert information. I advised the Flight Attendants of the situation and asked them to clean up and be seated for a normal landing. I made a PA announcement to the Passengers explaining the generator failure and the need to divert to ZZZ.
ASRSN:2098016.s: The crew experienced a Generator One Drive light during cruise, and the APU failed to start, requiring a diversion to ZZZ. ATC provided priority handling for the arrival, and the aircraft landed safely with no further issues.

ASRSN:2098026.n: Before flying the RNAV X into ZZZZ, we were given direct to the IF during arrival. This clearance left us with a steep descent profile to meet the company FAF standards. We elected to deploy the speed brakes and flaps to the 5 degree setting to expedite the descent. Up reaching 1500 ft. and continuing to slow, we extended the flaps to 10 at 205 Kias. We had a tailwind and were in and out of clouds giving us a bumpy ride and preventing the aircraft from slowing. With the bumps, we hit 207 Kias at one point, and I suggested we retract the flaps to 5. I placed the lever up to five and we decided to extend the gear instead. Then the FO called for flaps 15 at approximately 195 kts. I moved the handle to 15 and then noticed the flap gauge was showing flaps at 2. The gauge was 'frozen', in that no selected flap handle setting caused the flaps to move. We placed the lever at 2. The FO had begun a descent on the approach and she decided to perform a go-around. We received clearance to climb to 2,000 ft. and turn first to south and then west. We held a speed below max flap extension speed of 250, eventually settling on 225 KIAS. I believed that our situation would not allow us to safely land at ZZZZ because of the shorter runway length. A quick check in the FMS told us we were 300 NM from ZZZZ1. With our generous fuel load, we felt a diversion to ZZZZ1 was the best option. We coordinated for a climb to FL180, and set up a climb and cruise at 225 KIAS. After leveling off and proceeding on the clearance, we began the troubleshooting process using the QRC and FM (Flight Manual). We determined we had a flap disagreement situation. Running the QRC had us try moving the flaps to no avail. The checklist directed using the alternate flap extension procedure and hopefully getting to a final flap setting of 15. The non-normal landing distance table presented us with an estimated landing distance of 7400 ft. We flew the cleared arrival procedure for RWY XXR in ZZZZ1. On downwind, just prior to turning base to join the final, we started the alternate flap extension as we had discussed. We changed duties where I became the PF and my FO was PM. She performed the alternate extension. We finished all checklists and slowed the aircraft appropriately. I flew an uneventful ILS to a full stop landing. Our final calculated approach speed was 162 Kias, similar to flying a heavyweight ILS in gusty winds, an event we are very familiar with. After clearing the runway and taxiing to park, we began the process of debriefing all appropriate personnel, to include a Foreign Government representative. During approach into ZZZZ (RNAV (GNSS) Runway X), there were some cloud layer and tailwind that we were going through to get to our FAP altitude of 1500. As Pilot Flying, FO asked for flaps 1 and then 5 to slow down and descend. Entering more cloud layers, the speed was bumping 205 kts with flaps 10, after brief automation management decided to put up to flaps 5. After gear down was decided to slow down, Captain (PM) noticed flap indicator was 2 and would not extend or retract. Captain worried of the runway length. Altitude was approaching about 900 RA and FO mentioned might need to go around. Tower was notified of a go around, which we were given a heading and leveling of 2000 ft. FO took over both radio and flying while CA did the checklist and communication to dispatch and FAs. Captain suggested ZZZZ1 which had long runway and is a Maintenance base, and quickly imputed into the FMS for required distance. Decision was made to divert to ZZZZ1, no emergency declared but we asked to have emergency equipment standing by. Staying at 225 kts we climbed to FL 180 while following the QRH for flap disagreement checklist. PF and PM role was switched, and as a crew briefed and went over the process of alternate flaps procedure while preparing for ILS DME X Runway XXR from ZZZZZ STAR (XXR requested for longer runway). Flaps 15 with final speed of 162, Captain landed on runway safely. Hardstand XX was given after landing and taxied to ramp without emergency crews following. After parking, debriefed with Maintenance, Foreign federal aviation official (who asked us to fill a statement and took photos of FAA license and medical), Chief Pilot (talked to CA) and the ZZZZ1 airport official arranged and bused the passengers and crew to the terminal for a designated gate area.
ASRSN:2098026.s: During an RNAV arrival into ZZZZ, the crew encountered a frozen flap gauge and flap disagreement while managing a steep descent in bumpy conditions. They executed a go-around, diverted to ZZZZ1, and completed a safe landing using the alternate flap extension procedure.

ASRSN:2098028.n: Approach Control vectored us for a 4nm final visual approach to runway XX. This was a mile inside the final approach fix for the ILS XX. Using the 3 to 1 rule, we descended to 1200 ft. AFE. Tower informed us of a low altitude warning on their end and confirmed our correct altimeter setting. A stable approach was conducted followed by an uneventful landing. Vectored to 4 mile final visual runway XX. Used. 3-1 method and started a descent to 1200, in level change. Pressed alt hold so we wouldn't bust the 1000' AFE limitation in level change. Subsequently received a call from tower with low altitude alert. VFR severe clear, no safeties noted, and fully stable and configured, we continued to an uneventful landing.
ASRSN:2098028.s: The flight crew received a low altitude warning from Tower while descending to 1,200 feet AFE on a visual approach to runway XX. The alert occurred after the crew used the 3-to-1 rule and engaged altitude hold to avoid violating the 1,000-foot AFE limitation, but the landing remained uneventful.

ASRSN:2098069.n: Gear Retraction Failure - ZZZ-ZZZZThe crew met in the flight planning area at XA:15 for a XB:45 departure. We briefed as normal. The Captain was coming off of vacation, and the flying FO had flown recently, therefore, it was decided the FO would be the Pilot Flying (PF), the Captain Pilot Monitoring (PM), while I was the Relief Pilot. In preparation for our briefing I did not notice anything of concern regarding maintenance items, including recently closed out items. During the briefing we all agreed that we felt comfortable with the aircraft, and all other elements of the briefing.After the briefing we arrived at the aircraft before boarding and conducted our preflight duties. Being the Relief Pilot, I performed the preflight walk-around. During the walk-around I did not notice anything suspicious. We boarded and completed boarding on time. We concluded our preflight briefings with both the Captain and PF First Officer referencing the briefing items on the lanyard card to ensure nothing was missed, as well as completing an? guide for our oceanic crossing. At the conclusion of the briefings we ran the appropriate checklists as normal. We released the brake on time at XB:45, then waited at the gate for 10 minutes due to our slot time in ZZZZ. The push and taxi were normal with no non-normal indications and checklists completed before lining up for departure.Departure was from runway XXR, intersection 1, with a gusty right crosswind. I did not notice anything unusual during the takeoff roll. Shortly after the PF called for gear up I observed an amber EICAS message displaying GEAR DISAGREE, and shortly thereafter DOOR EICAS both in amber. The right main gear and door indications were illuminated with the nosewheel and left main gear indications extinguished. The noise and slight vibrations felt in the cockpit as we increased speed helped to confirm that we likely had the right gear down. We continued the takeoff climb as normal until we were given a heading and higher altitude from ATC. I quickly found the appropriate non-normal checklist. After the rest of the After Takeoff Checklist was completed, with a heading and altitude assignment from ATC, the PF turned on the autopilot. A quick discussion resulted in the PF (First Officer) remaining in control of the aircraft and working radios, while the PM (Captain) and myself went through the GEAR DISAGREE non-normal checklist. The non-normal checklist was completed with the gear handle in the up position until the checklist called for the gear down, when desired, prior to landing. Hydraulic pressure was at 3000 PSI on all systems, and quantities looked normal. At this point we had another short discussion which resulted in speaking to dispatch via Selcal about returning to ZZZ, to which they agreed was the best solution, then being connected to maintenance. In agreement amongst the pilots and maintenance we decided to lower the landing gear. With everything appearing normal, and the EICAS messages clearing, maintenance agreed the best course was to leave the gear down and complete a normal landing.Meanwhile, we were being given delayed vectors. After hanging up with maintenance and dispatch, and having completed the non-normal checklist, we convened. We decided to [advise ATC] with ATC, requesting CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) at ZZZ and further delayed vectors to increase our margin below maximum landing weight (320,000 lbs). While this was going on I was coordinating with the purser. We decided to have the purser prepare the cabin for an evacuation, even though the landing was expected to be normal. After speaking to the purser, essentially the same information was communicated to the passengers in a calming manner.Once again the pilots reconvened and, remembering we had a type-rated deadheading crew on board, decided to invite the deadheading Captain to the cockpit as a fresh set of eyes. After agreeing that everything was done appropriately and the plan going forward was sound he returned to his seat.We then briefed a normal descent and approach, ran the appropriate checklists, followed SOP communication and procedures with the cabin crew including their preparedness in case of an evacuation, and began heading back to ZZZ. The descent was normal with the approach consisting of a strong, gusty, right crosswind. Even so, the PF did a great job staying within stable tolerances and achieving a normal touchdown and breaking at approximately 312,000 lbs. We cleared the runway environment in a normal manner with CFR and maintenance nearby. In coordination with maintenance we shutdown both engines and then hydraulics so they could pin the gear. While arriving at the gate under tow, with the jet bridge on its way, the tug driver told us we had smoke coming from the right main gear. A normal deplaning was determined safe while we stayed in communication with the tug driver outside. A moment later maintenance came into the cockpit and explained it was hydraulic fluid leaking onto the warm breaks. At this point the hydraulics were already off, and the brakes had cooled from a level 4 to level 3 on the status page. The Captain received a call from the Chief Pilot a few minutes later and proceeded to debrief the Chief Pilot. With all parties in agreement we were released from duty for the night shortly after. Landing gear would not retract after takeoff. ZZZ-ZZZZ XB45 Departure. Preflight dispatch briefing indicated that we needed to delay on the ground for approximately 25 minutes to arrive within our ZZZZ slot time +/- 20 minutes. Ramp control indicated that we had a wheels up time of XC10 to help mitigate assist the excessive early ZZZZ arrival. The First Officer was PF (Pilot Flying) and the Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring) as this was my first flight in three months due to vacation. We released the brakes on-time and coordinated with ground crew to delay our pushback for 10 minutes. Pushed back at XB55 and once taxiing were number eight for departure. Takeoff clearance was issued around XC20. After liftoff, the PM retracted the landing gear. The Relief Pilot immediately pointed out that we had an amber GEAR DISAGREE and amber DOOR EICAS messages and lights as well as a green right GEAR down and locked light indication and the remaining left and nose gear lights extinguished. The PF took over the radios and continued flying as the Captain (PM) and Relief Pilot ran the Non-Normal GEAR DISAGREE checklist. The PF coordinated delay vectors and altitude of 12000 feet and 250 knots. The landing gear lever was placed in the OFF position IAW (In Accordance With) After Takeoff Checklist and then moved to the UP position IAW the GEAR DISAGREE checklist essentially completing that checklist. We checked the status page and Hydraulic pressure and quantity appeared normal. We contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control via phone patch. Maintenance Control checked the aircraft history for previous landing gear maintenance issues. The crew, Maintenance Control and dispatch all agreed that we would not attempt to cycle the gear down and then up to continue to ZZZZ. We decided to lower the gear while Maintenance Control was still on line. All three gear came down with normal indications. We all decided that the best course of action was to return to ZZZ and [request priority handling] with ATC and have CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) vehicles standing by. We had a deadheading Line Check Pilot come up to the cockpit as an extra resource. Satisfied with our decision to return to ZZZ, we briefed the Flight Attendants and Passengers and asked the Flight Attendants to Prep for Evacuation. We [requested priority handling] with ATC and began our approach to ZZZ. Below max landing weight at about 312,000 pounds, but still a heavyweight landing, the FO landed uneventfully on XXL with gusty crosswinds. We cleared XXL and were cleared to cross XXR. We stopped once clear of XXR and maintenance approached the aircraft to pin the landing gear. Maintenance asked us to shutoff our hydraulic pumps. We completed the Tow-in checklist and were towed into the gate. As we were getting towed in, the tug driver notified us that we had something leaking on our right gear and it was causing smoke. Although maintenance did not tell us that we had a hydraulic leak when they had us turn off the hydraulic pumps, we determined that the smoke was caused by hydraulic fluid leak on warm brakes and was not a fire risk. We deplaned the aircraft normally and maintenance boarded the aircraft and confirmed a center hydraulic leak. The Chief Pilot called me and I debriefed him on the incident. We all concluded that the crew should not continue to ZZZZ on a new aircraft.
ASRSN:2098069.s: The flight crew experienced a right main gear retraction failure shortly after takeoff from ZZZ, indicated by GEAR DISAGREE and DOOR EICAS messages. They returned to ZZZ for a safe landing with gear down, later discovering a center hydraulic leak caused smoke from fluid on warm brakes.

ASRSN:2098077.n: While at cruise flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, we got a IAS Disagree flag on both Primary Flight Displays (PFD's). This went away within about 60 seconds but happened again about 4 more times. During these events, we noticed an IAS difference of about 5kts between the Captain and First Officer (FO) sides. I contacted dispatch and got a phone patch with Maintenance. I briefed Maintenance on the situation and they suggested we continue but monitor the instruments. During this time, we reviewed the airspeed unreliable checklist but we still were not sure who had the unreliable airspeed. After the third event, I opened the airspeed window and slowed down and then sped up about 15 knots each. We observed that the FO IAS indicator did not move but the Captain and standby indicators followed the speed changes appropriately, telling us that the FO side was unreliable. I then swapped rolls to become flying pilot and gave the radios and monitoring pilot duties to the FO. We ran the checklist for unreliable airspeed. Once we started our descent into ZZZ1, the FO airspeed indicator dropped to 45 kts and the FO altimeter stayed about 1,000 ft. higher than the Captains and the standby. Once we completely lost those indications, I made the decision to [request priority] and continue to land at ZZZ1. We informed the Flight Attendants and Dispatch of the emergency status and landed without incident.
ASRSN:2098077.s: During cruise from ZZZ to ZZZ1, the crew experienced intermittent IAS Disagree flags and a 5-knot airspeed difference. After confirming the First Officer's instruments were unreliable via speed changes and observing total failure during descent, the Captain declared an emergency and landed safely at ZZZ1.

ASRSN:2098078.n: Shortly after takeoff the Fuel Filter Bypass Caution illuminated #2 engine side. Continued climb. Completed after takeoff checklist. Engaged the auto-pilot. First Officer ran the non-normal checklist. Transferred aircraft, radios to First Officer (FO). Leveled off at cruise altitude of 32000 ft. Contacted Dispatch, Maintenance Control via ACARS, phone patch. Discussed the fuel system, weather, terrain, and airport capabilities/services. We decided the safest course of action was a diversion into ZZZZ. Completed brief with flight attendants. Briefed passengers. Coordinated with ATC. Accomplished all briefings, setup, and checklists to include considerations, performance for an over weight landing. Descent and landing accomplished. No emergency declared. Taxied to remote parking.
ASRSN:2098078.s: The crew diverted to ZZZZ after a Fuel Filter Bypass Caution illuminated on engine #2 shortly after takeoff. They completed an overweight landing at 32,000 feet cruise altitude without declaring an emergency and taxied to remote parking.

ASRSN:2098135.n: While en route FL250, approx. 280 KIAS, vicinity of ZZZ, several ECAM messages appeared -- ENG 2 REVERSE UNLOCKED, ENG 2 FUEL CONTROL FAULT, ENG 2 FADEC A FAULT. It was difficult to assess messages because ECAM messages were continuously cycling making it difficult to read them. Engine appeared to be working normally but we were in an area reporting turbulence and experiencing turbulence. Descended to smooth area to determine we were experiencing turbulence and not buffeting, which is a possibility with reverser unlocked. For obvious reasons, diverted to ZZZ. Performed ECAM and QRH procedures. Brought #2 thrust lever to idle in accordance w ECAM for approach and landing. Engine appeared to operate normally. Landed overweight by about 3,500 pounds.Cause: Faulty warnings, but aircraft is still on maintenance hold as of this writing.
ASRSN:2098135.s: The crew encountered cycling ECAM warnings for Engine 2 faults while en route at FL250 in turbulence. They diverted, performed procedures, and landed overweight; the cause was faulty warnings, leaving the aircraft on maintenance hold.

ASRSN:2098167.n: After parking at the gate, the engines were shutdown. Shortly after shutdown the aircraft started to roll backwards away from the gate. Looking to my left I noticed the parking brake was not set. The parking brake was then set and the aircraft stopped rolling several feet from the original stop point.The left seat pilot not fully setting the parking brake before shutdown. The right seat pilot not recognizing the left seat pilot did not complete the task of setting the brake.Suggestions: Pilots should verify they hear and feel the audible click when setting the parking brake and ensure the brake on light remains illuminated before shutdown. Upon gate arrival, per the procedure of Captain shut down flow/checklist E175 the Parking brake set-I only saw the parking brake light on, likely due to not pulling the parking brake over the detent/click resulting roll back (after engine shut down). Upon restarting the engine, we are able to get back to the proper stop position, re-engage brakes and shut down successfully. The likely contribution factor is lapse in attention in a split second. Possible confirmation bias as part of verify lights on" versus "confirm lights on, be sure brakes are properly set" prior to moving onto other tasks.Suggestions: To begin with, self critique in: slowing down, take one thing at a time. Breathe. Even though it's a training event, have control over nerves and not to overthink. Procedurally we all know how to perform it, but be sure to do it right, do it safe. Take our time."
ASRSN:2098167.s: After engine shutdown at the gate, an E175 rolled backward because the left seat pilot failed to fully set the parking brake and the right seat pilot did not verify the task. The aircraft stopped a few feet away after the brake was set, attributed to a lapse in attention and confirmation bias.

ASRSN:2098203.n: Notified by flight deck right gear would not retract approx 20 min out... Confirmed would be returning to ZZZ shortly after and would indeed need to prep for evac right side gear locked down not sure would hold.Prepped cabin for landing and possible evac... Landed without incident. My assigned Jump Seat on the 767 is the overwing exit. During briefing with Captain we were told to remain seated after takeoff because of turbulence during climb out. After takeoff we noticed that the double chime for reaching 10,000 did not happen. I remained seated as instructed. Flight Attendant (FA) 1 came from the forward cabin and informed me that we will be returning back to ZZZ because of a landing gear issue. The Captain [requested priority handling] however he said there was no need for an emergency demo. My inter-phone was not working after takeoff. I was not able to hear the call from the Captain or Purser at the overwing exit. FA 1 stated that we had 10 min and that the Captain would make an announcement to the passengers. I immediately got up from my jump seat, took out my manual and went to my Emergency Procedures Chapter. I then started to prepare the cabin. Approximately 5 min later, I was now in the aft galley - Purser 2 called and spoke with FA 3. FA stated the Captain has [requested priority handling] and that we will need to brief the passengers. We all retrieved our safety equipment and proceeded to our assigned demo positions. The Captain made the announcement informing the passengers of our return to ZZZ Airport. Purser 2 began reading the emergency land evacuation brace position instructions and the crew performed the safety demo. After the demo I proceeded through the cabin, looking for able bodied passengers. I asked a deadheading ZZZZ based FA if he would take a jump seat in the aft cabin to assist with a potential evacuation. ZZZZ based FA 4 was seated in exit row XX, I asked if she would assist. I also briefed customers seated in exit row XY. I made a final walk through ensuring that all items were stored and seatbelts were fastened. We calmed fears and took our jump seats. The flight landed without incident. We taxied to end of runway and waited for approximately 15-20 min to be towed to gate. Amazing job was done by flight crew and operations crew.
ASRSN:2098203.s: A flight attendant on a Boeing 767 prepared the cabin for a potential evacuation after the right landing gear failed to retract and the interphone malfunctioned. The aircraft returned to ZZZ Airport and landed without incident, though the crew waited 15–20 minutes for a tow to the gate.

ASRSN:2098209.n: Cannot see out of 4L window, seal is broke around windows exposing inner door. Notified purser. During climb and descent the high pitch noise that is normally present was a lot higher pitch.
ASRSN:2098209.s: Cabin crew reported a broken seal on the 4L window exposing the inner door and preventing visibility. During climb and descent, the crew noted an abnormally high-pitched noise compared to normal operations.

ASRSN:2098264.n: There is a conflict at this airport between operators and the FBO when it comes to taxiing across the large ramp to get to the T-Hangars, instead of the taxi lane that goes around the perimeter. This is all non-movement area.In order to keep the peace, I've been doing my best to use the taxi lane, but they only just get onto the operators about this last week, and I've been cutting across the ramp for years. So muscle memory applied and I began to cut the ramp to go to my T-Hangar. The FBO engaged in reckless and hazardous behavior when they drove the golf cart out onto the ramp to block my passage. I was in a running aircraft, if I were looking down or anything else took my attention, that could have been an interesting altercation.I understand they are concerned with the risks involved with cutting the ramp, that's why I am going to work on using the taxi lanes exclusively. But creating risks and hazards on purpose is another thing altogether.
ASRSN:2098264.s: The pilot reported a conflict with FBO personnel while taxiing a running aircraft across a non-movement area ramp to a T-Hangar. The FBO driver created a hazard by blocking the pilot's path with a golf cart, prompting the pilot to commit to using perimeter taxi lanes exclusively.

ASRSN:2098273.n: My safety pilot and I took off ZZZ on Day 0 at approximately XA:30. I was (pilot in command) PIC and am the airplane owner. My plan was to execute 3 practice instrument approaches in VMC to maintain instrument currency/ proficiency. I had transitioned from the Tower frequency to ZZZ Departure and had just gone under the hood when my safety pilot asked about the moisture he was seeing on the windscreen. I looked up and saw oil streaming out of the oil door on the top cowling. Realizing that this could be a very bad situation, I immediately requested a frequency change back to ZZZ Tower and made the change. I asked ZZZ Tower for immediate landing and then, upon recommendation from my safety pilot, [requested priority handling]. ZZZ Tower cleared me to land and asked the nature of my [problem]. I advised oil on the windscreen. I performed an [priority] descent with power at idle and performed an uneventful landing. I taxied back to my hangar shut down and began the cleanup.The cause of the oil stream was a missing dipstick. (The engine is an IO-540-D4A5). I had interrupted my pre-flight and neglected to reinstall the dipstick after topping off with a quart of oil. I recently had changed my procedure from keeping the dipstick on the wing to hanging it from a hook on my bench (out of plain sight!) because I have a fresh paint job. The combination of interrupted pre-flight, hanging the dipstick on the bench and not having a spring on the oil door to keep it open when unlocked resulted in my error.Moving forward, I will return to keeping the dipstick on the wing near the pilot door when adding oil and installing a spring on the oil door to keep it open when not locked. These two items should alleviate a missing dipstick scenario.
ASRSN:2098273.s: The pilot and safety pilot experienced an oil leak from the top cowling during a practice instrument approach in a ZZZ aircraft due to a missing dipstick. The pilot requested priority handling, performed an idle descent, and landed safely after realizing the dipstick was left on the bench during an interrupted pre-flight.

ASRSN:2098278.n: I was pic of Aircraft X while upon landing and flare out, Aircraft Y crossed taxiway D & Runway 6 at COE. The aircraft in question did not announce that he was crossing Runway 6 @ D at COE while I was landing. I announced I was inbound for full stop landing Runway 6 at 10 miles out, 5 miles out, and short final as I was on the ILS Runway 6. As touching down, that is when the aircraft crossed. I landed on the 1000-foot mark. I did not go around because i was already stopping and had plenty of time to slow down. If I were to go around, my ground roll would have caused a close call or possibly crashing into the aircraft if I had not taken off in time. I believe that Coeur d Alene airport is in need of runway guard lights as well as a control tower as this airspace gets a lot of traffic and have multiple close calls here.
ASRSN:2098278.s: The PIC of Aircraft X landed on Runway 6 while Aircraft Y crossed the runway at taxiway D without announcing its position. The pilot did not go around, believing a missed approach would have caused a collision, and recommended installing runway guard lights and a control tower.

ASRSN:2098299.n: I was in the traffic pattern conducting a private pilot flight exam. We were one of 3 aircraft in the pattern. I witnessed an experimental aircraft turn an extremely early crosswind to downwind in front of the other C172 that was in the downwind of the traffic pattern. The tower was closed. All aircraft in the pattern were using left traffic and making position reports.The experimental aircraft caused the other C172 in the downwind to take prompt corrective action to avoid a near miss.I spoke with the C172 pilot on the ramp after the flight. He was visibly shaken and had to end his flight early due to his distress.The experimental pilot was in Aircraft Y. He refused to respond to any of my or the other C172 pilots queries about the situation on the CTAF.Aircraft Y was doing aerobatic type flight maneuvers while in traffic pattern and had no regard for any of the other traffic.
ASRSN:2098299.s: During a private pilot exam at a tower-closed airport, an experimental Aircraft Y performed aerobatic maneuvers and turned early in the traffic pattern, forcing a C172 to take corrective action to avoid a near miss. The C172 pilot ended his flight due to distress, while the experimental pilot refused to respond to queries on the CTAF.

ASRSN:2098308.n: While flying the missed approach for RNAV X at ZZZ and holding at ZZZZZ, had a near mid air collision with another aircraft entering the approach for ILS XX into ZZZ. Took evasive action to the right.
ASRSN:2098308.s: A pilot flying a missed approach for RNAV X and holding at ZZZZZ had a near mid-air collision with another aircraft entering the ILS XX approach into ZZZ. The pilot took evasive action to the right.

ASRSN:2098317.n: I performed various inspections on the aircraft, two of which required me to open the right hand hydraulic cowling door. I first performed an AD, followed by a visual of the hydraulic deck area and cleaning of the hydraulic deck area in accordance with the 30day airworthiness inspection. After the inspection and cleaning, the hydraulic cowl was shut and latches secured, I then moved onto the rest of the inspections. Prior to returning the aircraft to service, I had the pilot come out and visually inspect the engine chip plug installations, after that the transmission and engine cowlings were closed and a walk around was performed. The aircraft was then returned to service. After the aircraft had flown 1.6 hours, the Right hand hydraulic cowling came open in flight while the aircraft we on final to its home base, this resulted in the four main rotor blades striking the aft corner of the cowling. Aircraft safely landed and various inspections were performed, a new cowling was installed, blades repaired, and aircraft was returned back to service. During further investigation, it was noted that not all five of the fasteners were secured after maintenance was performed. It was also noted that this was not caught after three different walk arounds of the aircraft.
ASRSN:2098317.s: A mechanic failed to secure all five fasteners on the right hydraulic cowling after maintenance, which was missed during three walk-arounds. The cowling opened in flight on final approach, causing the main rotor blades to strike it, though the helicopter landed safely.

ASRSN:2098381.n: 1 box of radioactive medical shipment for a ZZZ [Airport] flight ABCD became mixed in with 8 boxes of radioactive medical shipments for a ZZZ1 [Airport] flight EFGH. A baggage handler dropped off 1 piece final destination ZZZ with the ZZZ1 shipments and it was loaded on the ZZZ1 flight.
ASRSN:2098381.s: A baggage handler mistakenly loaded one box of radioactive medical shipment destined for ZZZ onto a ZZZ1 flight, mixing it with eight boxes intended for that flight. This error resulted in the incorrect shipment being loaded on the wrong aircraft.

ASRSN:2098420.n: Within 25 mi of ZZZ airport the left fuel indicator started dropping rapidly. 1-2 Gal per minute of flight. We were abeem ZZZ1 so we made the decision to divert to ZZZ1.
ASRSN:2098420.s: The pilot reported a rapid left fuel indicator drop of 1-2 gallons per minute within 25 miles of ZZZ airport. While abeam ZZZ1, the crew decided to divert to ZZZ1.

ASRSN:2098429.n: Cleared 210 knots to PRINO intersection, then cleared for the approach. After PRINO and on final approach , we configured for the approach. Slowing to offset wake turbulence from the proceeding heavy aircraft, we slowed to 180 kts. Approach then told us to call Tracon upon landing.We should have requested a slower speed upon our first wake encounter
ASRSN:2098429.s: The flight crew, cleared for approach at 210 knots, slowed to 180 knots after PRINO to offset wake turbulence from a preceding heavy aircraft. The crew noted they should have requested a slower speed upon their first wake encounter.

ASRSN:2098452.n: Got to low on visual approach on 30L into MSP.Getting vectors into MSP 30L. ILS was out. Was cleared for visual. Was backed up with GPS appr. Received direct to fix. Then vectors to visual. I think between getting direct, vectors, configuring and slowing. The wrong alt was put in the FCP, or the low alt on the GPS was put in and a decent was started to early. When I became aware that we were to low on visual, I let the Captain know. I think the Captain became aware at same time and climbed back to a better alt. After climbing, ATC informed us they had a low alt alert and was everything ok. I told them all good.Suggestions: Be more aware of situational awareness on visual approach Planned the visual, backed up by the RNAV GPS Z 30L, as the ILS was out of service (OTS). We were cleared for the visual, and I looked at the chart to find a safe altitude to level off at. I used 1520 at EAGAN. (This was wrong, I should have used 3000 ft). I went to FLCH, and realized going through 2200 ft. that 1520 was too low. I hit altitude hold, and leveled off. ATC then gave us a low altitude alert. By this time we were aligned with final and saw the PAPI. We continued until on the normal PAPI glide slope to an uneventful landing. Cause: Used the wrong altitude from the chart Suggestions: Double check the altitude. I did brief the field elevation as part of the RNAV brief, but it didnt click that 1520 was too low when I used it. I dont go to MSP often.
ASRSN:2098452.s: The First Officer entered an incorrect altitude of 1520 feet instead of 3000 feet during a visual approach to MSP 30L, causing an early descent and a low altitude alert. The crew climbed to a safe altitude, confirmed the error, and completed an uneventful landing after aligning with the PAPI glide slope.

ASRSN:2098477.n: HYD SYS 1 LOW QTY Eicas Message displayed in flight. [Requested priority handling] as a precaution and made a normal approach and landing. ATC had trucks waiting. Airport Rescue and Firefighting inspected the aircraft and found no leaks. Aircraft taxied to the gate without further incident.
ASRSN:2098477.s: The crew received a HYD SYS 1 LOW QTY EICAS message in flight, requested priority handling, and executed a normal approach and landing. ARFF inspected the aircraft, found no leaks, and the flight taxied to the gate without further incident.

ASRSN:2098595.n: Today as a student pilot on my third solo flight flew a standard teardrop onto the 45 for a right downwind XX at ZZZ. Only three other planes making radio calls in the pattern at the time. Once established on downwind everything was setting up nicely. Turned right base continued to get on speed and set myself up for final. Turned final and made the radio call. At this point I began hearing mayday calls over the radio seven miles south of the field. I elected to continue landing to a full stop to clear the area for the mayday traffic if needed. I was over the runway almost to a flare when I hear go around and see a plane fly pretty close above me for the go around.I am not sure how we got so close to each other. I did not see them when flying the pattern or hear them on the radio. A lot of hecticness with the mayday calls could have resulted in me missing a call that they were on an extended final. Taking it personally I was hyper focused being on final and close to the runway. For the corrective action would be to divide my attention. Work on not hyper focusing. With experience this will come. Also making sure I'm still caged even when things start going another direction in critical phases of flight. Corrective action for other plane I think would be to announce position. I don't think I cut them off but if I did they never announced their position. I was the lower aircraft so I had priority. A lot was happening at once but will continue to get better with each flight!
ASRSN:2098595.s: A student pilot on a solo landing at ZZZ experienced a close call with an aircraft performing a go-around during a mayday emergency. The pilot attributed the proximity to hyper-focus and missed radio calls, noting the other aircraft failed to announce its position on extended final.

ASRSN:2098597.n: On Day 0 I was PIC of Aircraft X en route from ZZZ to ZZZ1 at flight level 410. At approximately XA:45 we had a 'CABIN ALTITUDE 10,000 FEET' alert. We immediately donned our oxygen masks and notified ATC that we needed a lower altitude. The first officer then read the QRH for the aircraft and completed all actions required therein as the I descended the aircraft. Upon passing flight level 250 [priority handling was requested] as we were unable to stabilize the leak rate. Emergency Descent Procedures were then initiated and a rapid descent to 10,000 feet was accomplished. Upon reaching 10,000 feet the cabin was depressurized and we notified ATC that we were no longer an Emergency Aircraft. We continued to our destination at 10,000 feet without further incident.
ASRSN:2098597.s: The PIC of Aircraft X en route at FL410 initiated an emergency descent after a cabin altitude alert indicated a leak that could not be stabilized. The crew descended rapidly to 10,000 feet, depressurized the cabin, and continued to the destination without further incident.

ASRSN:2098611.n: I flew two identical VFR flights below the floor of ZZZ Class C outer ring within two hours. The weather was clear at daylight with unlimited visibility. These were sight seeing flights under VMC conditions. The floor of the southeast sector is 1700 ft so I kept flying around 1400-1500 ft MSL. stayed away from the inner ring. The southwest sector floor of the outer ring raises to 2300 ft as the terrain rises to around 1000-1100 ft elevation with an antenna farm to the west. Being local I am very familiar with all landmarks within my flight path. So I've not refreshed myself with the sectional chart recently. So I took all floor levels as 1700 ft, and kept flying within this southwest sector below 1700 as well. I flew over the peak of the hills at 1300-1400 ft (200-400 ft AGL) and safely returned to my base ZZZ1. Even though I believe I have not created any safety risk in such a clear flying day by flying within couple of hundreds of ft AGL just to stay below 1700 ft, over these hills, this aircraft may have appeared very close to the ground. Had I refreshed myself with the charts to see this floor raising to 2300 ft from 1700 ft, I would have attempted to fly over the hills at 2100-2200 ft. instead of 1300-1400 ft. My lesson learned is 'Always refresh yourself with charts and latest information no matter how familiar you are with the environment you are flying.
ASRSN:2098611.s: A pilot conducting VFR sightseeing flights in a light aircraft inadvertently flew below the 2300 ft floor of the ZZZ Class C outer ring's southwest sector due to relying on memory instead of current charts. The pilot flew over hills at 1300-1400 ft MSL, realizing post-flight that updated chart review would have prompted a higher altitude to maintain proper clearance.

ASRSN:2098625.n: Aircraft had been given a clearance ZZZ-ZZZ1 at 040. This is a normal VFR route below 040 feet. I was working many 172's in this area that were VFR. I lost sight of this one being IFR. Just as they entered the 060 at 040 I climbed them to 060 and they confirmed with me that they had all the terrain in sight and continued on a slow climb to 060. An MIA warning on the strip would have been nice.
ASRSN:2098625.s: An air traffic controller lost sight of an IFR aircraft on a VFR route below 4,000 feet while managing multiple VFR Cessna 172s. The controller climbed the aircraft to 6,000 feet after terrain confirmation, noting that an MIA warning on the flight strip would have been helpful.

ASRSN:2098635.n: Aicraft X seen on Taxiway 1 after landing Runway XXR with a collapsed front gear and prop striking the asphalt, Pilot was notified to shut down engine. 30 minutes after, we were notified by airport authority that aircraft possible touched down short of the Runway in grass. Tower was not made aware of possible touchdown prior to Runway until some time later after the aircraft had been towed off the Taxiway and pilot was not available.
ASRSN:2098635.s: Aircraft X landed on Runway XXR with a collapsed front gear and propeller striking the asphalt, requiring engine shutdown. The airport authority later reported a possible short touchdown in grass, but Tower was not notified until after the aircraft was towed and the pilot unavailable.

ASRSN:2098642.n: Flew prior leg with no issues. During takeoff (at rotation) both Pilots experienced a deafening loud squeal in our headsets. I had to yell at the First Officer (FO) that I was essentially NORDO, with no intercom or ability to hear ATC. This was not like a stuck MIC, just a continuous very loud screech. It remained regardless of Audio Signal Processor (ASP) selection. The FO indicated that he was still (barely) able to hear and transmit to ATC. We used the procedure to troubleshoot and after several minutes, found that it was an issue with the intercom and not the VHF radios. Even when intercom was deselected, there was a screech, but it was tolerable enough to still hear ATC. We ACARS's Dispatch just in case we had any additional issues. The screech became somewhat intermittent but remained for the majority of the flight. No ATC deviations occurred. Upon landing at ZZZ, Maintenance was called to investigate the cause. They found that during pushback headset disconnect, part of the jack pin had broken off and caused a short in the intercom. The Maintenance Tech said this is starting to happen frequently, and especially in MAX aircraft as they are taller than the NG's and are pulled at a downward angle during disconnect that can break off part of the pin and remain inside the aircraft panel and thus cause a short.
ASRSN:2098642.s: During takeoff, both pilots experienced a loud headset screech causing the Captain to lose intercom and ATC audio. Maintenance later found a broken headset jack pin from pushback caused an intercom short, a recurring issue on MAX aircraft due to downward disconnect angles.

ASRSN:2098658.n: Pushed back from gate having briefed the ZZZZZ Departure for [Runway] XXR. After engine starts, new ATIS changed runways to XYR. Re-briefed the departure, changed the performance data values and ran the Departure Plan Checklist. We had an immediate take off after company and we flew through their wake turbulence at several points on the climb out until passing ZZZZZ. The FO and I commented on this while leveling off at the 8,000 ft hold-down. After ZZZZZ we took out the climb reduction and continued to climb. I continued to hand fly the departure and approaching ZZZZZ the autothrottles pulled the power back just like designed for the hold-down at 11,000 ft. In my mind, I thought the hold-down was 13,000 ft (ZZZZZ from [Runway] XXL Departure as initially briefed) and was confused when the power was reduced. I queried the FO and stated I'm not sure why the power is coming back now and continued to climb. Departure Control asked if we were going to level off at 11,000 ft and I immediately corrected back to 11,000 ft now completely understanding the error. Nothing more was said by Departure Control concerning the deviation and we continued to ZZZ1 uneventfully.Engaging the automation earlier certainly would have prevented the deviation as it worked as designed. Our close separation with company on the departure caused us to fly through wake turbulence and took some of our focus. Also running the Climb Checklist so close to a hold-down altitude slowed my recognition of what the automation was showing me. Day 0, I was the First Officer on company flight ZZZ to ZZZ1. Captain was flying this leg, and I was Pilot Monitoring. We had taken off from Runway XYR out of ZZZ. We were cleared to climb via the ZZZZZ RNAV Departure (FL190). As part of our pre-take off procedures, Captain briefed the entire departure. Captain was hand flying the aircraft during the climbout. As we approached waypoint ZZZZZ at an altitude of about 11,000 ft, Captain remarked about the autothrottles not advancing forward to maintain the selected climb airspeed. I immediately focused on the Flight Mode Annunciator trying to figure out why the autothrottles started to reduce thrust. Almost at the same at the time, ATC asked us if we were going to level off at 11,000 ft. That's when Captain and I realized that waypoint ZZZZZ has an altitude crossing restriction at or below 11,000 ft. By that time, I noticed that we had climbed to an altitude of 11,500 ft. Captain immediately descended 11,000 ft and we crossed ZZZZZ at 11,000 ft. After passing ZZZZZ, we resumed the climb via the SID without further incidents.
ASRSN:2098658.s: The Captain hand-flew a departure from Runway XYR and climbed to 11,500 ft, exceeding the 11,000 ft restriction at waypoint ZZZZZ due to confusion over a runway change and wake turbulence distraction. The crew corrected the altitude after ATC queried the level-off, noting that earlier automation engagement would have prevented the deviation.

ASRSN:2098674.n: Short final to 13L intercepting LOC Tower called low alt alert. Correct altitude and landed. Suggestion: Intercept final further out.
ASRSN:2098674.s: The pilot received a low altitude alert from Tower while intercepting the localizer on short final to runway 13L. The pilot corrected the altitude and landed safely, suggesting that intercepting the final approach course further out would prevent such alerts.

ASRSN:2098679.n: Flight XXX ZZZ to ZZZ1 took off from ZZZ Runway XX at XA:00. At XA:20, an ACARs message came through from the Crew, Engine #2 failed, divert to ZZZ.' Notified Superintendent of Dispatch, Maintenance, Chief of Dispatch and Chief Pilot. At XA:28, flight made a safe landing at ZZZ. Landed about 3,000-4,000 pounds over MLGW. While waiting for brake cooling, conferenced the Captain with the personnel mentioned above. Captain said he heard a 'bang', suspected a compressor stall. During post flight walk around, Captain reported damages on engine, elevator were discovered.Flight Crew handled the difficulty with grace. I, the Dispatcher, shall remain calm and collected. Assist the Crew to the best of my ability.
ASRSN:2098679.s: A dispatcher reported that Flight XXX experienced an Engine #2 failure shortly after takeoff, likely caused by a compressor stall. The crew diverted and landed safely at ZZZ, discovering damage to the engine and elevator during the post-flight inspection.

ASRSN:2098732.n: Our ACARS message stated we had one Wet Cell Wheelchair on board. We did not receive the Battery Powered Wheelchair or Mobility Device Tag" prior to pushback. I called ZZZ Operations asking for a copy of the form, and it took several minutes for them to determine that we did not have a Wet Cell Wheelchair boarded. This confusion added several minutes to our departure delay. It also didn't encourage confidence in our notification system."
ASRSN:2098732.s: The flight crew reported a departure delay caused by a discrepancy between an ACARS message indicating a wet cell wheelchair and the actual absence of the device. Operations required several minutes to verify the error, which the crew stated undermined confidence in the notification system.

ASRSN:2098748.n: Pushing back off of Gate XX in ZZZ we were cleared to push by ramp to spot XX. The tug driver began the push to spot XX. During the push back the tug disconnected from the aircraft. When the tug driver realized it, he commanded 'set brakes, set brakes, set brakes.' I immediately complied with the instruction. I quickly stepped on the brakes and stopped the aircraft. Once the aircraft was stopped I set the brakes. The tug driver told me that the tug had come uncoupled from the aircraft. He drove the tug up to the aircraft to reconnect and continued the push to spot XX. Then I received a call from the Purser that one of the Flight Attendants (FAs) had been injured. I then spoke to the injured FA and she said that she had strained her back and that she would not be able to do her duties. I asked if she wanted to go back to the gate. She said yes. We coordinated a return which was gate XY. We went back to the gate and removed the flight attendant from the aircraft. During our second flight of the day (ZZZ-ZZZZ), and after receiving an aircraft swap and reviewing its subsequent release revisions (now revision 4) all briefings and checklists were completed.We were ready for pushback and had gotten clearance to pushback from Gate XX in ZZZ. During the middle of pushback the tug operator excitedly said, 'SET BRAKES! SET BRAKES! SET BRAKES!'After the initial startle, the Captain got on the brakes and abruptly stopped the aircraft. The tug driver then explained that the aircraft became disconnected and that's why he told us to set brakes.After the abrupt stop and parking brake set, we received a call from the cabin that a Flight Attendant (FA) had fallen and may need assistance. While this was going on the ramp crew had simultaneously reattached us and we resumed getting towed to our assigned spot. FA stated that her back was tweaked and discussed the incident with the Captain. Captain and FA concluded that she could not continue her duties and needed to be check out by a medical professional.We coordinated a gate return and the available gate was XY on the other side of the terminal. We completed after start checklists and coordinated with ramp and Ground Control to taxi to our new gate.Upon reaching our new gate we parked the aircraft and completed our parking checklists without any further incident.
ASRSN:2098748.s: During pushback from Gate XX in ZZZ, the tug disconnected from the aircraft, causing an abrupt stop and a Flight Attendant to strain her back. The crew returned to Gate XY to remove the injured crew member, while the tug was reconnected to complete the tow to the assigned spot.

ASRSN:2098755.n: As the ramp crew began to disconnect, the ramp tower advised that we had not completed a 'full push' although the push seemed normal. The CA advised the push crew that we would need to push back more while I sought clarification from the ramp controller. During the process of reconnecting, apparently at some point the aircraft began to roll away from the tug. I believe the ramp crew may have advised the Captain to release the brakes for capture without having a strap attached.
ASRSN:2098755.s: During pushback, the aircraft rolled away from the tug while the crew attempted to reconnect after a ramp tower advisory. The pilot suspects the ramp crew instructed the Captain to release brakes for capture before the tow strap was attached.

ASRSN:2098757.n: Captain silenced GPWS warning and ignored 'whoop whoop pull up.'I was PM on the first leg to ZZZ and XX_20 XXXXXX was PF. Captain got four red lights on his approach into ZZZ. He continued the approach. To the best of my memory we got glideslope" alerts three times. The last glide slope alert was followed by 'whoop whoop, pull up.' Captain was hand flying at this point and reached his hand up and pressed the 'below G/S P-inhibit.' I believe we are under 500 feet at this point. The landing was the hardest one I have felt in my short time in the 737 on the line. Captain apologized and said 'this aircraft will humble you.' He told me his landing was not a good example." Demonstrating an approach and landing to an IOE student in visual conditions with gusty turbulent winds. As I verbally teaching the approach stable at 1000 ft. and 500 ft., at or below 200 ft. a sinker occurred and was immediately corrected the glide slope aural sounded on short final, since the flight was in VMC conditions with a displaced threshold and reestablish on a 3 degree glide path, I silence the aural and continued to land on the runway. This was thoroughly debriefed after shutdown. The GPWS was never shutdown and there was no Pull Up warning at anytime.
ASRSN:2098757.s: An IOE student and Captain conducted a visual approach in a 737 with gusty winds. The Captain silenced a glide slope alert below 200 feet to continue landing, resulting in a hard touchdown that was later debriefed.

ASRSN:2098788.n: We were 5 miles in trail of a heavy A350 on a visual approach for 28R. We were advised by the Tower Controller that there would be a heavy aircraft taking off of 28R between us and the A350 flight ahead. The A350 cleared the runway at Tango intersection and the heavy aircraft lined up and began their takeoff roll while we were descending through approximately 500 ft. By the time we approached the touchdown zone we were experiencing significant wake turbulence from the landing heavy aircraft in from of us and the jet blast from the heavy departing in front of us. We landed safely but because of the tight spacing between us and the heavy aircraft we trailed, the heavy aircraft that departed in front of us - the safety margin narrowed considerably.
ASRSN:2098788.s: The crew on a visual approach for 28R encountered significant wake turbulence and jet blast while descending through 500 ft due to a heavy A350 landing ahead and a heavy aircraft departing between them. Although they landed safely, the tight spacing between the three aircraft considerably narrowed the safety margin.

ASRSN:2098800.n: Received NO DG (Dangerous Goods) message. Pushed off gate, received RAMP DIDN'T SECURE HAZMAT message. Was concerned why we didn't receive a Final DG Summary per SOP. Returned to gate, and HAZMAT was secured properly. Talked to Load Planning and verified a Final DG Summary was not required. Received a no DG (Dangerous Good) ACARS message and pushed on time. Upon starting second engine received another ACARS message from the Load Planner that HAZMAT was not secured properly, which we were unaware we had. Called Operations and received direction to taxi back into the gate. Apparent confusion between Operations and Load Planning on whether a dangerous goods summary was required and why direction to pull back into gate was given. Rampers opened up doors and secured HAZMAT as directed. We waited another several minutes to receive confirmation that a DG summary was not required and then re-accomplished checklists and coordinated with ATC for the delayed departure.
ASRSN:2098800.s: The flight crew returned to the gate twice due to conflicting ACARS messages and operational confusion regarding unsecured hazardous materials and required summaries. Ramp personnel secured the cargo, but the departure was delayed while the crew verified procedures with Load Planning and Operations.

ASRSN:2098836.n: A safety person alerted me to a Dangerous Goods (DG) situation, after reading the most recent company bulletin. The most recent company bulletin details updates to the procedure for securing baggage. However, the safety person indicated that a Ramp Assistant Manager recently called DG personnel to find out if they could secure DG with a wheelchair or stroller. The DG desk allegedly said this was permissible, which I do not believe it to be.
ASRSN:2098836.s: A safety person reported that a Ramp Assistant Manager was allegedly told by DG personnel that securing Dangerous Goods with a wheelchair or stroller was permissible. The reporter disputes this advice, noting it contradicts recent company bulletin updates on baggage securing procedures.

ASRSN:2098875.n: In route to Kuwait from ZZZ, we experienced GPS jamming. Standard operating procedures were followed, and checklists completed for the associated EICAS messages. Getting closer to Kuwait we noticed thunderstorm activity on our route of flight. We opted to begin descent later to avoid them, as well as requesting and being cleared for 15 track miles left of course. After passing the weather we were given a descent, and clearance to proceed direct to KFR. We then were given additional vectors, then direct IVETA and clearance for the ILS Y 15R. Approaching IVETA with roll mode in LNAV, the aircraft did an unexpected turn to the right prior to IVETA. The Captain, PF, selected heading mode and manually controlled the heading of the aircraft. At that time, our ANP value was fluctuating well above the RNP value. I, PM, told ATC we had degraded GPS accuracy. We were then given vectors to intercept the final approach course for ILS 15R and proceeded as expected. Our ANP value was above RNP all the way to the parking stand, and our map showed the airplane in the incorrect location. Cause: GPS spoofing.
ASRSN:2098875.s: The flight crew experienced GPS spoofing en route to Kuwait, causing degraded accuracy and an unexpected turn while in LNAV mode. The Captain manually controlled the aircraft, and ATC provided vectors to intercept the ILS 15R final approach course for a safe landing.

ASRSN:2098878.n: For the latter half of this flight to LAS we were given an assigned speed for metering of .76 MACH, then to 270 kt., and finally 280 kt. We were given the increase from 270 to 280 kt. while being handed off from LA Center to Las Vegas Approach Control. Upon checking in with Approach Control, my FO (First Officer) and I noticed that we were approaching the fix PEHTY which has a speed of 250 kt. However, we were adhering to the previously assigned speed of 280 from LA Center. The Controller abruptly and angrily gave us a heading, speed, and altitude to fly AND gave us a phone number to call for a pilot deviation. When asked why, the Controller said this was their only way to get LA Center's attention because they were constantly sending aircraft at too high of a speed into Las Vegas airspace. This was highly distracting, inappropriately timed, and extremely unprofessional on the part of the Controller. Pilots should only be notified of a violation once they are safely on the ground. I called the phone number and spoke with a supervisor. He reiterated that this was indeed what they are doing to get LA Center's attention as all other methods have been unsuccessful. I was also told that we are not the only ones they have done this to. They are doing this to 3 - 4 aircraft PER DAY.Flying the assigned speed of 280 from LA Center as told. There has to be another way for the FAA to work out their differences between LA Center and Las Vegas Approach Control other than violating pilots. I feel that we should be left out of the equation. During the RKSTR 3 Arrival into LAS, Los Angeles Center began stepping us down in altitudes and assigned a speed of 270 kt., then subsequently a speed of 280 kt. a few minutes later for spacing." My understanding of our current clearance was to descend via the arrival except maintain 280 kt. Los Angeles Center then handed us off to LAS Approach. The Captain, pilot flying, and I were aware that we were rapidly approaching the PEHTY fix with a published 250-kt. constraint, and we discussed whether it applied in this scenario or not, especially since we were still well above 10,000 ft. We were both under the impression that Los Angeles Center needed us to keep the speed up for traffic management as the controller had previously indicated. Furthermore, by this time we were so close to PEHTY that it likely would have been impossible to slow the aircraft from 280 to the 250 kt. constraint while also descending to meet the altitude constraint.Since we were in the frequency handoff process, we elected to obtain clarification from the new ATC Controller. Due to task priorities and frequency congestion, we passed PEHTY before I, pilot monitoring, could check in with the new Controller. At the soonest opportunity, I checked in with LAS Approach, and I additionally emphasized "280 assigned speed" to prompt them for clarification. I intended to use plain English if this did not suffice. Without any hesitation or opportunity to resolve the discrepancy, LAS Approach immediately assigned us a slower speed and a vector off the arrival course, informed us of a possible pilot deviation, and instructed us to copy a phone number. When the Captain inquired of the reason for this alleged deviation, LAS Approach indicated there is a trend of aircraft being handed off from Los Angeles Center to them at incorrect speeds, and that LAS TRACON has elected to use the pilot deviation process as a tool to remedy this trend of alleged misunderstanding between the two ATC agencies, and between ATC and flight crews.After ensuring a safe arrival and landing, and after completing all post-flight duties, the Captain and I participated in a phone call with LAS TRACON to discuss the scenario. The LAS TRACON representative reiterated the same narrative of a trend of aircraft being handed off by Los Angeles Center at incorrect speeds. This occurs almost daily among various commercial operators. Furthermore, he verbalized not knowing "what else to do" to get Los Angeles Center's attention (paraphrased) to remedy this discrepancy between the two agencies, and LAS TRACON has now elected to use the pilot deviation process as one method to obtain resolution.I wholeheartedly believe that using a pilot deviation is an unacceptable, unfair and extremely unprofessional method to resolve the root cause of an obvious disparity between ATC agencies. We are professional pilots who have dedicated our lives to the pursuit of excellence, and who understand the meaning of "descend via" and "climb via." Our FOM and training programs build upon this by ensuring we are prepared to execute these procedures as part of qualification and re-currency. Thus, we routinely execute these procedures without fail, often multiple times per day, on almost every flight when part of a published SID or STAR. This specific scenario feels like a trap. While trying to comply with the controller's intent, and due to ongoing dispute between two ATC agencies, now flight crews are set up for potential violation. Surely there must be more appropriate avenues to resolve this, such as working groups, committees, or liaison dialogue between the two agencies.I believe the fact that Los Angeles Center needed and assigned altitudes and speeds other than as published on the arrival was a causal factor. We know what the intent of a "descend via" clearance is when it is given with no ambiguity, but when combined with assigned altitudes and speeds, it can lead to a confusing situation in a dynamic environment. Also, frequency congestion and ATC controller handoff at a "choke point" such as PEHTY are causal factors, in my opinion, due to limited time and ability to obtain clarification.First and foremost, the disparity between Los Angeles Center and LAS TRACON must immediately be resolved. This is the root cause of this scenario. Immediate resolution is crucial via more appropriate methods other than compiling multiple pilot deviations on multiple commercial operators. In general, I believe standard phraseology should be adopted to remedy and prevent this scenario. No matter what location or published arrival, I recommend something like "cancel previously assigned speed, descend via..." will eliminate any ambiguity in this situation. I am fully aware that is what "descend via" is meant to convey, but it is NOT sufficiently concrete in my opinion when you consider that we had just been given varying altitudes and speeds contrary to "as published." Clearly I'm not alone, as the Las Vegas TRACON representative indicated this is a continuing and increasing trend among various operators into LAS."
ASRSN:2098878.s: Pilots flying an arrival into LAS maintained a 280 kt speed assigned by LA Center, passing the PEHTY fix before clarifying with Las Vegas Approach. The controller issued a pilot deviation notice to pressure LA Center regarding frequent speed discrepancies, a practice the crew deemed unprofessional and caused by inter-agency conflicts.

ASRSN:2098913.n: Before fix ULINA we were GPS spoofed. The aircraft showed us on course. However, we were not. We soon began receiving messages stating the aircraft was downgrading to other forms of navigation before finally giving us an 'UNABLE RNP' message. Our navigation display showed our aircraft was on course, while also stating we were 20 miles off course, full scale. Cairo Control had previously told us to contact Amman Control at the fix ULINA. Because we were suddenly not where the aircraft believed it was, we did not call ahead in time. When we got in contact with Amman, we requested radar vectors until we were able to verify our position. GPS jamming and spoofing continued for roughly 25 minutes and GPS reception was eventually restored. We followed EICAS and GPS spoofing protocols. No loss of aircraft separation occurred. Cause: External malfeasance.
ASRSN:2098913.s: The flight crew experienced GPS spoofing before fix ULINA, causing navigation discrepancies and an 'UNABLE RNP' message that delayed contact with Amman Control. They requested radar vectors to verify position while GPS jamming persisted for 25 minutes, but no loss of separation occurred due to external malfeasance.

ASRSN:2098946.n: During preflight, a gross Mx (Maintenance) oversight was discovered related to the pitot static system.While accomplishing the preflight, we got multiple spurious ECAM alerts, which required maintenance intervention. The aircraft seemed to think it was airborne. After multiple power swaps, system resets and additional maintenance crew member discussions, it was determined that a pitot line had not been connected, despite the fact that the aircraft was signed off as airworthy. After the maintainers corrected the issue, making the aircraft fit for service, I discussed the events with them. I advised them that I would hold off writing a safety report until after they filled me in on what led up to this oversight. I have heard nothing.
ASRSN:2098946.s: During preflight, the flight crew discovered a maintenance oversight where a pitot line was disconnected, causing spurious ECAM alerts and false airborne indications. Although the aircraft was signed off as airworthy, maintenance corrected the issue, but the crew has not yet received an explanation for the error.

ASRSN:2098959.n: Climbing out of ZZZ [airport] I was the pilot flying, at approximately 12,000' the AT (Autothrottle) and AP (Autopilot) kicked off and followed up with a AVNX MAU (Modular Avionics Unit) 3A fail message with several other associated messages. I continued flying by hand and talking on the radios while the captain ran the QRH. We decided to level off and let ATC know we would need to be vectored for a few minutes while we ran some checklists for the issues. We could tell that the speed brakes were at least 75% deployed due to being able to feel them in the flight deck. I notified the Captain, we decided to slow to 190 knots and work our flaps 2 in to see if the speed brakes would stow, they did not. The captain elected to request priority handling because we didn't know what type of control issues might arise during the approach. At this time while hand flying, there was noticeable control difficulties with the ailerons. We decided to turn back to ZZZ due to icing conditions towards our destination, and the QRH telling us to stay clear of icing. The captain ACARS dispatched to let them know, he takes to the flight attendants and passengers to let them know what was happening and why we would be returning. We called operations to ensure they knew we were coming back and to have a gate open with ramp personnel waiting. The QRH directed us to call for the flight control malfunction descent and landing checklist. Due to not having ADS 3 (Automatic Data System), FMS 2, and GPS 2 we elected for a transfer of flight controls for the descent and landing. After setting everything up for the approach we let ATC know we were ready for the approach. Both the approach and landing were uneventful. Upon landing we cleared the runway with a left turn and stopped to talk to ground. The safety equipment was surrounding us and asked if we needed assistance. We told them we could taxi to the gate and received our taxi clearance. I then called the OPs and they told us they were pushing back another aircraft despite our situation. After a few minutes the ramp team came and got us to our gate. Climbing out of ZZZ [airport] at approximately 12000 ft EICAS MSG AVNX MAU (Modular Avionics Unit) 3A FAIL with several other associated messages. FO (First Officer) was the flying pilot. I had him continue as flying pilot and also elected to have him take the radios as well. I ran the AVNX MAU 3A FAIL QRH procedure. The procedure said avoid icing conditions. There were icing conditions in ZZZ1 so I told my First Officer to tell ATC that we would plan on going back to ZZZ. First Officer informed me that it felt like the speed brakes were deployed. The speed brake indication on the EICAS was amber. The speed brakes were definitely deployed. We slowed to 190 kts in order to select flaps 2 to see if the speed brakes would stow. They did not. At that time I advise ATC due to not knowing exactly what position they would be in during landing. My First Officer advised ATC. I ACARS dispatch to let them know what was going on. I advised the flight attendants the nature of the situation and told them we wouldn't need the brace commands or the planned evacuation checklist. I advised the passengers of the situation and told them to plan on a normal landing that might seem a little fast due to the flight control malfunction. I advised them that they would see personnel around the plane after landing. I also advised them to follow the instructions of the flight attendants after landing. I called ops in ZZZ to let them know we were a priority aircraft returning to ZZZ. The QRC procedure directed us to Flight Control Malfunction Decent & Landing Checklists as well. The checklist gave us our appropriate speeds and landing configuration as well as a 1.2 malfunction factor. Due to us not having ADS 3, FMS 2, and GPS 2 I elected to fly the approach. After briefing and setting up the approach we transferred the flight controls to me as the flying pilot. First Officer told ATC we were ready for the approach to XXR into ZZZ. The approach and landing were uneventful. We exited at Taxiway 1. The safety equipment were there for us and asked for our intentions. We said we were good to taxi to the gate. They followed us to the gate. Ops didn't have a ramp crew meet us at the gate. First Officer called the ops frequency and asked for a ramp crew to marshal us into the gate. He was told our crew was working another flight and they would be over after they were done. He reminded ops that we were a priority aircraft and had personnel there waiting with us. The ramp crew then came out after a couple more minutes to guide us in.
ASRSN:2098959.s: The First Officer and Captain experienced an AVNX MAU 3A failure, autopilot disconnect, and deployed speed brakes at 12,000 feet while climbing from ZZZ. They returned to ZZZ due to icing and control difficulties, executing a manual flight control malfunction landing with priority handling.

ASRSN:2099010.n: After releasing the brakes when we were ready for pushback, we received an ACARS message saying Notification Form WARNING. It said 'pilot in command must acknowledge receipt of final notification form using the dangerous goods acknowledgment code prior to aircraft movement.' That was the first time we were aware that we had dangerous goods onboard our aircraft. Previously, upon initialization we received a no dangerous goods planned message on the ACARS. After we pushed back and brakes set, I called our Dispatcher/Load Planner to question him about dangerous goods. I also asked the Ground push crew about dangerous goods and they acknowledged that yes, dangerous goods were boarded. After I spoke with our Dispatch he pushed the Final Dangerous Goods Summary to our printer and at that point we sent the dangerous goods acknowledgment code and got the acknowledgment. The rest of the flight was uneventful.
ASRSN:2099010.s: The flight crew discovered dangerous goods onboard after receiving a warning ACARS message during pushback, despite an earlier "no dangerous goods" notification. After confirming the cargo with ground staff and dispatch, the crew acknowledged the final form, and the flight continued uneventfully.

ASRSN:2099011.n: We were given instructions to taxi to [Runway] XXL via [Taxiways] 1/2/3 and hold short [Runway] XY. After holding short XY, we were instructed by Ground to continue and monitor Tower. Approaching XXL we noticed a Citation Longitude holding short of [Taxiway] 3 on [Taxiway] 4. Although they were delaying some departures due to the weather, we had received no delay notifications or instructions to hold for the other aircraft and pulled forward along the curved center line, and stopped short of XXL. We heard no communications from Aircraft Y at this point. Arrivals were slow to come in and after a few minutes Tower asked an aircraft on final to slow to get traffic out. Aircraft Y made their first transmission stating they were ready to go. Tower then asked if they could 'get by the airliner' which Aircraft Y immediately said yes and began to pull forward and come right of their centerline in attempt to get around us. I saw what was happening and informed the Captain who was noticing the same thing. I also quickly made a radio call saying 'there's not enough room' but it may have been blocked by Tower issuing the planned sequence for departures. The Captain noticing what was going on took over the radio and said we would have to turn out of the way to allow Aircraft Y room to get by us. Tower then changed us to line up and wait for immediate take off. Aircraft Y response was annoyance that we were going first and continued to insist that they could fit between us and the edge of the taxiway. We departed and continued to ZZZ without incident.If there is a doubt, there is no doubt. Even a small perception that something is unsafe should have everyone stop and evaluate the situation further. Tower should not have relied on just one aircraft to decide if there was enough room to taxi by us. Later investigation about Aircraft Y led us to discover that the aircraft has nearly 70 ft. wingspan with rather large curved winglets. From our view point there was no way it could safely taxi between us without hitting our nose or departing the taxiway. There was plenty of opportunity for Tower to have us hold short elsewhere or use [Taxiway] 5 for departure after turning us out of the way. I also would be very curious to know Company's reaction to a pilot putting their aircraft and passengers at risk just to go first and having a pilot argue about a perceived safety issue. Coming several feet off centerline, attempting to squeeze between a very large transport category aircraft, risking collision with a fully loaded 737-900ER and coming close the edge of a lighted taxiway with tall edge lights and then getting upset when a safety issue is called into question are very concerning to me. If the Captain had not pressed the issue I believe that damage to one or both our aircraft would have occurred.
ASRSN:2099011.s: The 737-900ER crew and a Citation Longitude experienced a near-collision on the taxiway when Tower cleared the Citation to pass the airliner despite insufficient space. The Citation pilot attempted to squeeze between the 737 and the taxiway edge, but the 737 Captain intervened to avoid a collision, prompting the Citation to depart after the airliner.

ASRSN:2099076.n: Taking off RWY XX flex power was set, had engine failure number 2 engine at around 40kts, rejected and taxied off, fire rescue trucks were called to check out the plane, taxied to gate. Compressor stall on number 2 engine at 40 knots on takeoff roll from runway XX in ZZZ. Rejected takeoff and excited runway. Fire trucks inspected and we had no visible damage so they escorted us to the gate.
ASRSN:2099076.s: The crew rejected takeoff on Runway XX at 40 knots due to a compressor stall on engine 2. Fire rescue inspected the aircraft, found no visible damage, and escorted it to the gate.

ASRSN:2099087.n: We were cleared to taxi to Runway X in ZZZ after deicing in snowy conditions. We taxied north from the ramp on Taxiway 1 and at a slow ground speed I initiated a left turn on Taxiway 2. After completing the turn the airplane continued to turn left and the airplane also kept moving forward with the brakes fully applied.
